questions.passage: Should paramedics be authorised to prescribe antibiotics at the scene of an emergency?
questions.question: Which is the strongest argument FOR allowing paramedics to prescribe antibiotics?
options: Timely antibiotic administration in sepsis cases can significantly reduce mortality
Paramedics already carry a wide range of medications in their ambulances
Patients trust paramedics and would likely accept their prescriptions
GPs are sometimes unavailable, so someone else needs to fill the gap
questions.correct: Timely antibiotic administration in sepsis cases can significantly reduce mortality
questions.explanation: This provides a direct clinical justification grounded in patient outcomes. The other options are weaker — carrying medications doesn't justify prescribing, patient trust is not a clinical reason, and GP unavailability doesn't establish paramedic competence.

questions.passage: Three patients — X, Y, and Z — are assigned to three rooms numbered 1, 2, and 3. Patient X is not in room 1 or room 2. Patient Y is in a room with a higher number than Patient Z. Each patient is in a different room.
questions.question: Which room is Patient Z in?
options: Room 1
Room 2
Room 3
Cannot be determined
questions.explanation: Patient X must be in Room 3 (not 1 or 2). Patient Y has a higher room number than Z, so Y is in Room 2 and Z is in Room 1.

questions.passage: A rapid strep test has a sensitivity of 95% and specificity of 90%. In a school clinic, 20% of children presenting with a sore throat actually have strep throat.
questions.question: If a child tests positive, what is the approximate probability they have strep throat?
options: About 35%
About 50%
About 68%
About 83%
questions.explanation: Of 100 children with sore throats: 20 have strep (19 true positives). 80 don't (8 false positives). P(strep|positive) = 19/(19+8) ≈ 70.4%. Closest is 68%.

questions.passage: In a group of 100 patients: 55 have hypertension, 40 have diabetes, 20 have both conditions, and 25 have neither condition.
questions.question: How many patients have hypertension but not diabetes?

questions.passage:
A hospital's quarterly report shows:
- Emergency department waiting times increased 25%
- Staffing levels decreased by 10%
- Patient satisfaction scores dropped from 82% to 71%
- Bed occupancy rate rose from 88% to 97%
questions.question: Which inference is best supported by the data?
options: The hospital should hire more administrative staff
Increased bed occupancy and reduced staffing likely contributed to longer wait times and lower satisfaction
Patient satisfaction is not affected by wait times
The hospital is becoming more efficient
questions.correct: Increased bed occupancy and reduced staffing likely contributed to longer wait times and lower satisfaction
questions.explanation: Higher occupancy (97%) and lower staffing (-10%) logically explain increased wait times (+25%) and decreased satisfaction (82%→71%). These data points together support this causal inference.

questions.passage: All patients with Type 1 diabetes need insulin. Some patients who need insulin also need glucose monitoring. No patient who monitors glucose should skip meals.
questions.question: Which conclusion definitely follows?
options: All Type 1 diabetics should not skip meals
Some Type 1 diabetics should not skip meals
Some Type 1 diabetics need glucose monitoring
All patients who skip meals do not monitor glucose
questions.correct: Some Type 1 diabetics should not skip meals
questions.explanation: Some patients needing insulin also need glucose monitoring, and glucose monitors should not skip meals. Since Type 1 diabetics need insulin, some of them may need glucose monitoring and thus should not skip meals.

questions.question: Which referral source showed the most consistent quarter-on-quarter growth?
options: GP
Self
Hospital
School
questions.explanation: GP referrals increased every quarter: 120→135→150→160. Self-referrals also grew but more slowly in Q3. Hospital had a dip in Q2. School declined in Q3-Q4.

questions.passage: Should hospitals implement a policy of mandatory flu vaccination for all healthcare workers?
questions.question: Which is the strongest argument AGAINST the mandate?
options: Mandatory vaccination may violate individual bodily autonomy and informed consent principles
Flu vaccination is not 100% effective in preventing transmission
Some healthcare workers have religious objections to vaccination
The cost of administering vaccines to all staff is significant
questions.correct: Mandatory vaccination may violate individual bodily autonomy and informed consent principles
questions.explanation: This raises a fundamental ethical concern about personal autonomy and consent, which is a serious counterargument. The other options are weaker — imperfect efficacy is a reason for other measures not against vaccination itself, religious objections can sometimes be accommodated, and cost is relatively minor.

questions.passage: Of 90 medical students on placement: 60 are at a metropolitan hospital, 35 are at a rural hospital, 15 are at both locations, and 10 are at neither location.
questions.question: How many students are at the metropolitan hospital only?

questions.passage: Four doctors — Dr. Evans, Dr. Foster, Dr. Grant, and Dr. Hughes — are on a rota covering four consecutive shifts on Monday. Dr. Hughes works before Dr. Evans but after Dr. Grant. Dr. Foster does not work first or last.
questions.question: Who works the first shift?
options: Dr. Evans
Dr. Foster
Dr. Grant
Dr. Hughes
questions.explanation: Dr. Grant before Dr. Hughes before Dr. Evans. Dr. Foster can't be first or last. So the order must be Grant, Foster, Hughes, Evans. Dr. Grant works first.
